checkpoints: The input document sent to the policy engine needs fields like user{id,roles,department,clearance}, action, and resource{id,owner,department,sensitivity} — enough for all three models to evaluate against one shared payload.

Each model uses a different subset of that payload: RBAC only needs user.roles, ReBAC only compares resource.owner against user.id, ABAC checks user.department/clearance against resource.department/sensitivity.
The decision returned is {allow, reason}, where reason is the part everyone forgets but matters most — it turns an opaque 403 into a decision an operator can read immediately.

The boundary is absolute: the app (enforcement point) only gathers context, POSTs the input, and maps allow/deny to 200/403 — it holds no roles or rules of its own and can't answer "why" beyond echoing the reason.

Because rules never live in the app, adding/editing a rule means editing one policy file (auditable, version-controlled) with NO app redeploy — the same input document even supports a future fourth rule.

Edge case: coerce types right at the enforcement point before sending — e.g. clearance arriving as a string from a header must be converted to a number, or a numeric comparison silently fails and produces an unexplainable deny.

Edge case: treat a missing decision (policy failed to load, network dropped, empty response) as deny — fail closed, never default to allow — since a missing decision is otherwise indistinguishable from a legitimate deny at the HTTP layer.
The contract has four parts: what a workload presents, what it gets back, how its identity is encoded for a peer to read, and how it renews.
A workload proves who it is with a platform-issued bootstrap credential (e.g. a service-account token or equivalent orchestrator-issued identity) presented to the internal CA (the issuer).
In exchange it receives a short-lived certificate and matching private key, signed by that shared CA.
Identity does not live in a request header (a self-declared string); it lives in the certificate's CN/SAN, ideally a SPIFFE URI SAN independent of any DNS name.
A peer never trusts a self-declared identity — it verifies the presented certificate against the shared CA first, then reads identity out of the CN/SAN field.

Rotation works via overlapping validity: a new certificate is ready before the old one's TTL runs out, and a mesh sidecar or SPIFFE/SPIRE agent performs issuance and swap automatically — the app process never restarts or observes a gap.

Certs are deliberately short-lived because a smaller TTL shrinks the window a leaked key is useful, and expiry-by-schedule reduces reliance on revocation lists/OCSP — the trade-off is this only works with full automation, which is why it belongs to platform infra, not app code.

The single biggest risk sits in the CA's private key: whoever signs is trusted unconditionally, so a leak lets an attacker mint a valid cert for any identity — mitigated by keeping the key in an HSM/KMS, keeping the root CA offline, and issuing day-to-day through a short-lived intermediate CA to bound the blast radius.

Escaping in one handler is only as strong as the most careful handler and protects only the sink its author had in mind — as the codebase grows, safety depends on every developer remembering to escape correctly every time in every new place, and there's no backstop the day a raw query or an unescaped call is added elsewhere.
A WAF middleware at the edge closes that gap by being a single choke point that runs before any route, inspecting all three input surfaces (query string, headers, body) uniformly.

With a WAF: the payload is checked against the rule set at the edge, a match is short-circuited with a 403 {status: blocked, rule}, it never reaches the backend, and the 403 itself never echoes the payload back (which would create a reflected-XSS sink).

Without a WAF: the same payload is stopped only if it happens to go through the one handler that was carefully escaped — a different path (new endpoint, raw query, outbound call) has nothing standing in its way.

The WAF is one layer of defense-in-depth — it buys time and blocks most known patterns (and some zero-days) but does not replace parameterized queries or output encoding at the application layer; it's the outer wall, not the vault door.

Adding "Sign in with Google" is identity brokering, not a rewrite of authentication: it lives entirely in the Keycloak realm's configuration — register Google as an Identity Provider (one-time admin task with client id/secret) and add the button to the login screen.

Keycloak runs the full OAuth dance with Google behind the scenes; once Google confirms identity, Keycloak issues its OWN JWT signed with the realm's existing key, exactly as it does for the username/password flow.

That's precisely why none of the three services (orders, billing, notifications) needs a line changed: each only ever validated tokens offline against the realm's JWKS, and that JWKS/signing key/realm are unchanged — the services can't know whether the login went through Google or a password.
The access token is the one that travels to orders/billing/notifications as a Bearer token — it authorizes API calls, and each service reads its roles/scope to decide what the caller may do.
The id token never leaves the client; it carries identity claims like sub, email, and preferred_username so the browser can greet the user and knows who is logged in.
A resource service consuming the id token to gate access would be a mistake — that is not what it is for.

The trust boundary the three services rely on (offline signature validation against the realm's public key) is exactly the same before and after Google is wired in; identity brokering changes who authenticates the human, not how the API trusts the resulting token.
Admin-can-do-anything is RBAC — granted by role membership, the coarsest model, simply checking whether "admin" is in the role list.
Same-department-and-sufficient-clearance is ABAC — granted by a conjunction of attribute values (department matches AND clearance >= sensitivity).
Edit-your-own-document is ReBAC — granted by the relationship between the subject and that specific object (owner == user id), the only model that can express "your own" anything.
You do not commit the whole system to one model — you pick the model per rule.
The three rules coexist as independent allow blocks OR'd together over a single `default allow := false` base, so access is granted the instant any block matches.
Each block needs to know nothing about the others — they are fully decoupled from one another.

Safety comes from deny-by-default: a forgotten or buggy rule fails closed, producing a visible 403 instead of a silent hole — unlike hand-rolled if-checks scattered across controllers where a missing branch silently lets a request through.
The richness of expression comes from freely mixing RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC inside that one safety net.
Rotation re-wraps only the DEK — it never touches the already-stored ciphertext, no matter how many terabytes of data exist.
The KEK's sole job is to wrap and unwrap DEKs; it never encrypts application data directly.
The wrapped-DEK blob carries the KEK version tag (e.g. `vault:vN:...`).
The KMS keeps old key versions live so DEKs wrapped under v1 still decrypt correctly, while new writes wrap under v2.
This makes rotation an O(1) KMS operation, not proportional to data volume.
A lazy rewrap is an optional background job that re-wraps old DEKs to retire deprecated key versions.
The single-shared-key-per-table model instead needs a full O(table) decrypt-and-re-encrypt pass, requiring both old and new key live at once, with blast radius covering the entire dataset.
With offline JWT validation, the access token stays valid until it expires (`exp`) even after the user is disabled, because the API never calls the identity provider back per request.
That gap is exactly the tradeoff that buys O(1) validation and linear scaling with instance count without adding load on the identity provider.
Introspection closes the gap instantly by asking the identity provider on every request whether the token is still alive.
Introspection costs a network hop plus per-request load in exchange for that immediate revocation.
Pick introspection for sensitive admin APIs where a revoked token must die immediately; pick offline validation for high-traffic APIs where a few minutes of lag is acceptable.
To shrink the gap without paying for a call on every request, use a short access-token lifetime plus refresh-token rotation, where each refresh invalidates the prior token.
That refresh-rotation caps exposure at exactly `exp`, since a revoked session cannot keep minting new access tokens.

For dangerous operations (delete, grant permission, payment), require step-up MFA by checking the `acr` claim, so a still-valid token isn't strong enough unless the user re-authenticated at a higher assurance level.

Vault's KV v2 secrets engine wraps every read response in two nested envelopes: the JSON body is `{ data: { data: {...values...}, metadata: {...version...} } }`, so the actual secret values sit under `response.data.data.data` when read through axios (whose own `.data` holds the parsed body).

A successful `vault kv put` together with a raw HTTP GET against `/v1/secret/data/my-app` returning the value proves Vault itself, the token's read permission, and the original write are all fine, which narrows the fault to how the client code parses the JSON response.

`response.data?.data?.DB_PASSWORD` stops one hop short of the real value: it resolves to the inner envelope object `{ data: { DB_PASSWORD }, metadata: { version } }`, which has no `DB_PASSWORD` key of its own, so the optional chain quietly evaluates to `undefined` instead of raising a traversal error.

The `if (!password) throw new Error(...)` guard is functioning exactly as intended as a fail-fast check — it just cannot tell a genuinely missing secret apart from a response read at the wrong nesting depth, so it throws a misleading "not found" error for what is really a parsing bug.

The fix is one more `.data` hop — `response.data?.data?.data?.DB_PASSWORD` — and the resulting nested chain should not be flattened or "simplified" later, because it mirrors Vault's real KV v2 envelope structure (outer HTTP wrapper, inner data, sibling metadata) rather than being redundant defensive code.

Fetching the secret inside `TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync`'s `useFactory` means a parsing bug in `VaultService.fetchDatabasePassword` surfaces as an application boot crash rather than a contained runtime error, which is why the symptom reads as a startup failure instead of a scoped, easily isolated bug.

The bug can be pinned down and prevented from regressing with a fixture test: feed the function a response shaped like the real KV v2 body (`{ data: { data: { DB_PASSWORD: 'x' }, metadata: { version: 1 } } }`) and assert the extracted value equals `'x'`, plus a second case where `DB_PASSWORD` is genuinely absent and the fail-fast `Error` still throws.

The append() method performs the tail read (orderBy "e.index" DESC + getOne()) and the subsequent insert as two separate, unserialized database statements, with no transaction and no row lock connecting them.

When two POST /events requests run concurrently, both can execute their tail read before either one has inserted, so both see the same last row and therefore compute the identical index (last.index + 1) and the identical prevHash (last.entryHash).

Because index is the primary key, the second of the two concurrent inserts throws a duplicate primary-key error; if index were not uniquely enforced, both rows would instead point their prevHash at the same parent, producing a fork instead of a single linear chain.

Appending to a hash chain is conceptually "extend the chain by one link," an operation that is inherently serialized — whoever inserts next must see the true, current tail, which a plain tail-read-then-insert sequence does not guarantee.

A GET /verify that walks the rows in index order will hit the point where the expected prevHash-to-entryHash linkage breaks and report a broken chain; this report is a symptom of the concurrency-induced fork, not evidence that any row was tampered with or edited by an attacker.

The minimal correct fix is to make the tail-read-then-insert sequence atomic: wrap append() in a transaction (e.g. this.dataSource.transaction(...)) and read the tail under a pessimistic write lock (TypeORM's setLock("pessimistic_write"), i.e. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE under the hood), so a second concurrent transaction blocks on that read until the first commits and only then sees the new tail.

The fix can be proven by firing N concurrent append() calls and asserting that the resulting rows have contiguous indices from 0 to N-1, each row's prevHash equals the previous row's entryHash, and GET /verify returns valid: true.

Reading identity from raw `x-user-id` / `x-user-roles` request headers and trusting it outright means the policy engine's decision is only as trustworthy as the input the enforcement point feeds it — any caller can simply set `x-user-roles: admin` on the wire and be granted access, since the engine faithfully evaluates whatever claim it is handed.

Authorization identity must be derived from a verified source, such as a signed JWT validated upstream by a guard/interceptor, or a service-mesh identity, and the policy input should be populated only from those trusted claims — never straight from raw, client-supplied headers.

Wrapping the policy-engine call in a try/catch that returns `{ allow: true }` on both a thrown network error and a missing result is a fail-open design: a single outage or misconfiguration of the decision point silently turns into a full authorization bypass for every request through this endpoint.

The failure mode should be fail-closed instead: an unreachable policy engine or a missing decision result must produce a denial surfaced as 403 or 503, never an implicit allow that passes the request through.

"The engine returned no decision" and "the engine explicitly denied" are two different signals that should not be conflated — a missing result typically means the policy package failed to load, not that access was denied, so treating them the same hides an availability problem behind a false sense of security.

Both the unverified-identity issue and the fail-open issue are MUST-FIX authorization-bypass defects rather than style nitpicks, because the trustworthiness of the input and the failure-mode behavior together are what constitute this middleware's actual security posture.

A regression test that sends a spoofed `x-user-roles: admin` header from an unverified caller and asserts a 403 once identity is sourced from a verified claim instead demonstrates that the spoofing hole is actually closed.

A test that mocks the policy engine as unreachable and asserts the endpoint returns 403 or 503, never 200, demonstrates that the fail-closed behavior genuinely holds rather than being assumed from reading the code.
